title: The Wow! Signal Hasn't Been Settled in Nearly 50 Years: It Looks Like an Alien Call, but No Second One Ever Came
dek: That 72-second narrowband hydrogen-line signal from 1977 has never repeated, and it falls short of the threshold for evidence of an alien civilization; its legacy isn't an answer but a reminder that in a noisy universe, the distance between detection and proof is an entire galaxy.
why: Anyone hoping for a verdict will be disappointed; if you want to understand how a single anomaly becomes evidence or fails to, this episode gives a complete framework for judgment.
who: Podcast listeners curious about SETI's evidentiary threshold, science fiction writers, astronomy new-media editors; also suited to anyone misled by clickbait alien news who wants to be set straight.
skip: The channel and Nebula membership promotion at the end can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: The 72-second length comes from Earth's rotation
points.body: Big Ear was a transit telescope: it didn't turn to track targets, but relied on Earth's rotation to sweep the whole sky overhead. A point source fixed on the celestial sphere crossing the beam naturally takes about 72 seconds — exactly 1/1200 of a day. So the duration doesn't mean the sender deliberately spoke for only 72 seconds; what really matters is the gain curve: a real source enters the beam, grows stronger, leaves the beam, grows weaker. The Wow! signal matched all of that, and later terrestrial-interference explanations have to pass this test first.

points.h: 6EQUJ5 is an intensity curve, not a code
points.body: 6EQUJ5 is the signal-strength reading in Big Ear's early print format: each symbol represents an observation window of about 12 seconds, and the digits and letters indicate the factor above background noise. In time order they are 6, 14, 26, 30, 19, 5 — strong in the middle, weak at the ends, like a brightness curve written sideways. Renormalized to 1–100, that's 17, 40, 74, 86, 54, 14. The host's quip is worth remembering: if the aliens' first sentence looks like a failed software activation code, that's also a reasonable opening.

points.h: It hugs the hydrogen line, yet is off by 50 kHz
points.body: 1420 MHz is the radio spectral line of neutral hydrogen, a natural landmark of the universe's most abundant element, and the frequency SETI most often assumes for a call. The Wow! signal's frequency, because Big Ear had its master oscillator set 0.1 MHz too high, has two corrected values: 1420.356 MHz or 1420.456 MHz; the true hydrogen line is about 1420.406 MHz. Both are only about 50 kHz off, as if deliberately avoiding hydrogen noise while using the hydrogen line as a coordinate. But that position is also full of natural hydrogen-cloud signal sources, and cleverness versus coincidence cannot be distinguished by frequency alone.

points.h: One horn received it, the other didn't
points.body: Big Ear had two side-by-side feed horns. A source fixed on the celestial sphere, swept by Earth's rotation, should enter the two horns in succession and be recorded twice. The Wow! signal appeared in only one horn, and the records don't say which, so the sky left two candidate positions. Possible reasons include: the source itself was bright for only a very short time, a narrow beam happened to graze it, or the interference came from nearby. All later searches — including the 2022 Breakthrough Listen search for Sun-like stars in the candidate region using Green Bank and the Allen array — heard no repeat. The lack of a second detection is the core reason it can't enter the confirmed list.

points.h: Terrestrial interference and satellites are hard to mimic
points.body: Earth is noisy, but a true candidate signal has to pass the 72-second profile test: an ordinary aircraft crossing the beam wouldn't last so conveniently long; a low-orbit satellite usually crosses in just a few seconds. For a satellite to do it in high orbit, via a side lobe, or in a special orbit would require a chain of coincidences. Terrestrial transmissions are banned in the internationally protected 1420 MHz band, but illegal equipment or faulty electronics could produce out-of-band signals that leak in through antenna side lobes. There's also an effect called interstellar scintillation that can briefly brighten a distant signal, but that requires an amplified source to exist first. None of these explanations is perfect, which is exactly why the puzzle survives.

points.h: Magnetars could pump a hydrogen cloud into a maser
points.body: Research based on Arecibo archives has spawned a natural explanation: some high-energy transient — say a magnetar flare — pumps atoms in a cold neutral hydrogen cloud into population inversion, briefly turning the cloud into a natural microwave maser, much like a laser amplifying microwaves. This can explain several things at once: the signal came from space, was near the hydrogen line, was strong enough, yet appeared only once; the hydrogen cloud was glowing when the first horn swept past, and had gone dark by the time the second horn came. The host says this is his personal favorite because it solves multiple puzzles with one mechanism, but it remains a speculative path with no conclusive evidence.

points.h: Becoming a discovery requires passing four gates
points.body: If such a signal is received again in the future, calling it a true technosignature would require at least four conditions: one, it repeats at the same position, so we know it's still there; two, telescopes at two different locations receive it simultaneously, ruling out Earth interference; three, the signal carries modulation, encoding, or mathematical structure, rather than being a mere carrier wave; four, known natural processes are ruled out one by one. Historically, when pulsars were first discovered they were nicknamed "little green men," showing that nature can perfectly impersonate intelligence. The right posture isn't to take sides in belief or mockery, but to allow excitement and then do your utmost to prove you're fooling yourself.

points.h: Its legacy is a window that was too narrow
points.body: The Wow! signal appeared for 72 seconds in exactly the form early SETI hoped to know — narrowband, near the hydrogen line, strong enough, shaped like a real source in the sky — and then nothing more. It showed what a great discovery might look like before the evidence is sufficient. The host's landing point: the galaxy is 100,000 light-years wide and billions of years old, and even the largest civilization is just a flickering spark within it. If civilizations don't spread, don't transmit often, and don't often point their beams at us, the Fermi paradox may not exist. With that 1/1200 of a day, the Wow! signal briefly brought that possibility before human eyes.

terms.def: A radio telescope fixed in orientation that doesn't track celestial objects, relying on Earth's rotation to sweep the sky through its beam.
The spectral line emitted by neutral hydrogen near 1420 MHz, the most common radio landmark in the universe.
The quiet radio band between the hydrogen line and the hydroxyl lines, where SETI often assumes civilizations would call.
A microwave-band stimulated-emission amplification mechanism that can produce narrowband strong signals like a laser.
A secondary reception direction outside the main beam, through which strong interference can leak into a telescope.
An observable signal or trace indicating a non-natural technological origin, the search target of SETI.

facts.k: Two corrected values for the Wow! frequency

facts.v: In 2022 Breakthrough Listen used two telescopes and found no repeating signal

quotes.text: Science is happiest when things are either confirmed or discarded. The Wow signal has managed to neither.
Being near the hydrogen line also means nature has plenty ways to be involved.
A one-time signal can be interesting, but it cannot carry the weight we would want for a claim as huge as extraterrestrial intelligence.
A possibility that cannot be confirmed, repeated, or tested gets weaker with time. It may remain interesting, but does not become evidence merely by aging well.
even the mightiest civilization we have ever built is still only a flickering spark against the immense scale of a galaxy 100,000 light-years wide and billions of years old.
The most efficient way to talk loudly across interstellar space may look to the recipient like a random, non-repeating glitch, but it also pushes back into the idea as a deliberate contact strategy.
And again, the 6EQUJ5 signal is not text we got. It's just a measurement of brightness over six measured intervals.
That is not cynicism. That's how you avoid fooling yourself in a universe full of noise.
